## Now put something underneath it

[Lesson 55](55-capstone-solo-melody.qmd) gave the setup phrase a shape of its own. Here it gets company. The
same eight pitches become the melody of a two-bar model with a bass and an inner
harmony, all three on one shared timeline.

Something changes as soon as the bass can move. The setup buffer held a single
E2 under everything, which is why nothing could clash. Give the bass a G in bar
2 and the same A4 that sat comfortably over E minor is now doing a different job
over a G chord. Notes don't have fixed meanings. Chords give them meanings, and
the bass has a large say in what the chord is.

Encode the three roles as independent structures. Your data should read like a
score model: a reader sees what each part does at a given beat without tracing
`play` and `sleep` calls. This project leans on the Roman-numeral engine from
[Lesson 28](../06-chords-and-harmony/28-diatonic-chords-roman-numerals.qmd), the voice-leading checks from [Lesson 31](../06-chords-and-harmony/31-voice-leading-optimisation-problem.qmd), and the timelines from
[Lesson 47](../10-texture-and-arrangement/47-independent-voices.qmd).

## Melody, bass and inner harmony on one clock

Global starts put all three roles on one coordinate system. Threads let the
melody and bass advance independently, and an end-time check confirms they agree
about how long the passage is. Two of the melody notes fall outside the chord
sounding under them. Can you find them before you look?

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 70

melody = [
  {note: :e4, start: 0.0, duration: 1.0},
  {note: :g4, start: 1.0, duration: 1.0},
  {note: :a4, start: 2.0, duration: 1.0},
  {note: :b4, start: 3.0, duration: 1.0},
  {note: :d5, start: 4.0, duration: 2.0},
  {note: :b4, start: 6.0, duration: 1.0},
  {note: :a4, start: 7.0, duration: 0.5},
  {note: :g4, start: 7.5, duration: 0.5}
]

bass = [
  {note: :e2, start: 0.0, duration: 4.0},
  {note: :g2, start: 4.0, duration: 4.0}
]

harmony = [
  {notes: chord(:e3, :minor), start: 0.0, duration: 4.0, symbol: :i},
  {notes: chord(:g3, :major), start: 4.0, duration: 4.0, symbol: :III}
]

define :play_events do |events, synth_name, amp|
  use_synth synth_name
  cursor = 0.0
  events.each do |event|
    sleep event[:start] - cursor
    play event[:note], release: event[:duration] * 0.85, amp: amp
    cursor = event[:start]
  end
end

ends = [
  melody.last[:start] + melody.last[:duration],
  bass.last[:start] + bass.last[:duration],
  harmony.last[:start] + harmony.last[:duration]
]
raise "parts end at different times" unless ends.uniq.length == 1

in_thread { play_events melody, :piano, 0.85 }
in_thread { play_events bass, :fm, 0.5 }

use_synth :hollow
harmony.each do |event|
  play_chord event[:notes], release: event[:duration] * 0.9, amp: 0.35
  sleep event[:duration]
end
```

Both A4s are the outsiders. One passes between G4 and B4 over E minor, the other
between B4 and G4 over G major. Neither belongs to the chord underneath, and
both sound ordinary, because a passing tone earns its place through timing, not
membership. Your validator should point at them and let you explain them.

Three event counts, eight, two and two. One shared boundary at beat 8. That's
the architecture.

## Break the alignment check

1. Shorten the final G4 from `0.5` to `0.25`. The assertion stops the program
   before a note sounds, because the melody now ends at 7.75. If your source
   really has a quarter-beat of silence there, put the silence in the data.
   Don't lengthen the note before it and don't weaken the check.
2. Restore the duration and change the first melody note from `:e4` to `:f4`.
   Against E minor, F4 grinds. The pitch-class report will flag it, and the
   report can't tell you whether the pitch, the chord label, or your analysis is
   the thing that's wrong. Only the source can.
3. Restore E4 and move the bass up an octave, to `:e3` and `:g3`. Chord
   identities and durations hold still while the gap between bass and harmony
   closes. Listen to the inner register before you touch any amplitude.

## Why the timeline is the interface

One shared timeline is what lets the parts stay separate. Each role owns its
events; every start and duration uses the same origin and unit. That buys you
independent rendering, bar validation, muting and transposition. It also avoids
the fragile design where the bass's sleeps become the clock for the melody, so
one local edit silently shifts every other voice.

Chord checking is pitch-class arithmetic. Reduce sounding notes with `note % 12`
and compare against the active chord. A mismatch invites you to look at the
beat: passing tones, suspensions and anticipations all produce deliberate
mismatches whose timing explains them. Expose those notes; never flatten them
into the triad.

Whole-piece alignment is necessary and nowhere near sufficient. Two voices can
both end at beat 32 with a three-beat bar and a five-beat bar hidden inside one
of them. Partition each role by measure, count rests as elapsed time, and assert
the meter before you combine anything.

Once the reports are clean, this same data supports arrangement without your
rewriting a note. The three roles can take different synths, registers, pans and
effect depths. Mute one and hear what the others were carrying.

## Arrange a source you can check

Take a sixteen-to-thirty-two-bar song, hymn or keyboard miniature whose three
roles you can each follow. Deliver separate structures on one timeline, with
metric checks for every active voice in every bar, a report comparing each
sounding pitch class against the active chord, and an annotation for every
intentional non-chord tone.

Start with strict alignment and plain synths, so attacks, rests, overlaps and
clashes have nowhere to hide. Arrange afterwards. All three roles stay
independently mutable and muteable, and no synth, pan or effect choice belongs
near the score data.
